sections.title: Paris events
sections.content:
• The Getdown + aja monet — today, 16:00. Salle des concerts, Cité de la musique, 221 avenue Jean-Jaurès, Paris 19e. About 3h05. €28 full / €24 under 26. The seven-piece Getdown is built around Laurent Coulondre on Hammond B3 and Arnaud Dolmen on drums, with piano, flute/voice, alto sax and trumpet; poet aja monet opens with Justin Brown, Micah Collier and Brian Hargrove. The Philharmonie still lists the concert, but its ticket selector currently shows no selectable seats, so treat this as resale/walk-up territory rather than guaranteed availability. Philharmonie

  • Émile Parisien / Yaron Herman / Linda May Han Oh / Prabhu Edouard — “Floating” — Tuesday 1 September, 20:00. Salle des concerts, Cité de la musique. About 2h30. €35. Melissa Aldana & Levi Harvey Trio open. This is musically the strongest near-term jazz bill for your taste — melodic modern writing with a very legible quartet texture — but the Philharmonie now shows it as sold out / waiting list, so it is mainly worth joining the list rather than planning around a normal ticket. Philharmonie

  • Les Traversées du Marais — Friday 4 to Sunday 6 September. 27 cultural institutions plus 5 satellite galleries across the Marais; free, reservation advised. The 12th edition is organized around “Dialogue(s)” across disciplines, cultures and generations, so it works better as a browseable weekend than as one fixed show: museums, archives, libraries and performance venues all contribute short events. Ville de Paris

sections.title: CS and AI development: visual evidence is becoming a scheduled resource
sections.content:
Two August papers make a useful pair because they attack opposite failure modes in multimodal inference: sometimes a model needs to look again; sometimes it needs to stop carrying visual evidence sooner. The systems question is not simply “more or fewer image tokens?” but when visual information is worth paying for.

ReGround starts from a reasoning failure rather than a compression target. The authors re-examined 2,510 samples across four benchmarks and found a recurring signature: during multi-step reasoning, attention over image tokens becomes more concentrated, then spreads again when the image is re-injected. Their key result is that blind re-examination is not enough — re-inserting the image without a targeted diagnosis can hurt. ReGround therefore trains a model to emit a self-diagnosis when it suspects grounding loss, then selectively re-injects the original visual evidence. It does this without an external vision tool or architecture change. Across eight benchmarks and two VLM backbones, the authors report consistent gains with modest overhead. ReGround

The second paper asks the inverse question: when does token reduction actually make inference faster? Its break-even accounting includes the cost of the routing decision, shared work that every policy must still perform, and which pipeline stages can actually be skipped. In a 30-example pilot, two autoregressive routing probes were slower than the full baseline even with state reuse. A lightweight post-vision predictor did produce significant latency reductions on RTX 3090 and A100, but the more interesting result is structural: a cheap pre-vision rule can avoid preprocessing and the vision encoder entirely. On A100, that opportunity outweighed a nearly eightfold larger downstream token reduction from the post-vision policy. The paper also warns that its quality numbers are conditional on examples the full model already answered correctly, not end-to-end benchmark accuracy. Break-even study

The common design principle is evidence scheduling. A static token budget treats every sample and reasoning step alike. These papers instead make visual computation conditional on where you are in the pipeline and whether the model currently lacks grounded evidence. ReGround spends more visual compute only after diagnosing drift; the break-even study shows that pruning pays only when the saved stages exceed the routing overhead. Both are recent preprints, so the reported benchmark and latency results should still be treated as author-reported rather than settled.

sections.title: Technical idea: Robin Hood hashing flattens probe-length tails
sections.content:
Robin Hood hashing is an open-addressing hash table that deliberately makes unlucky keys less unlucky.

In ordinary linear probing, a newly inserted key walks forward from its home slot until it finds an empty position. That can produce a long-tailed distribution of probe lengths: some keys sit almost exactly where they belong, while a few get pushed very far away. Robin Hood hashing changes the collision rule. Each resident entry has a probe distance — how far it has travelled from its ideal slot. When an incoming key collides with a resident that has travelled less far, the newcomer steals the slot and the displaced resident continues probing. In slogan form: take from the “rich” key that is close to home and give the slot to the “poor” key that has already travelled farther.

The point is not to minimize the total number of probes so much as to compress their variance. Celis, Larson and Munro's original work reports fewer than 2.6 probes on average for successful searches even when the table is nearly full, while unsuccessful searches grow only logarithmically in the table size. Modern implementations can also exploit probe-distance ordering to terminate some failed lookups early: once the search has travelled farther than the resident key at the current slot, the missing key could not have survived insertion past that point. Celis, Robin Hood Hashing

The trade-off is insertion work. Collisions may trigger a chain of swaps, so writes can be more expensive than plain linear probing. That is often a good exchange when the goal is predictable lookup latency rather than the cheapest insertion path — a general systems pattern worth remembering whenever tail behavior matters more than average behavior alone.

sections.title: Non-CS science: a thousand-year coral record puts modern El Niño in context
sections.content:
A new Science study used Galápagos coral skeletons as a monthly-resolution thermometer for the eastern tropical Pacific, extending the El Niño record roughly a thousand years before industrial warming.

Corals are useful here because they accrete calcium-carbonate layers while incorporating chemical signatures that vary with seawater temperature. The team combined living and ancient corals from the Galápagos, where eastern-Pacific El Niño anomalies are especially strong, to reconstruct sea-surface-temperature variability before modern instruments existed. According to Nature's report on the paper, strong El Niño events have occurred more frequently over the past century than in the pre-industrial millennium, and the last four decades contain variability outside that earlier range. Nature

Why this matters is not just “warmer ocean = stronger El Niño.” ENSO is a coupled feedback between equatorial Pacific water temperatures, trade winds and atmospheric convection. Stronger warm anomalies can reorganize rainfall and storm tracks far beyond the Pacific, raising drought, flood, wildfire, crop and ecosystem risks in different regions at the same time. The result also addresses a measurement problem: climate models have difficulty reproducing every part of that wind–water feedback, while direct observations are sparse before the twentieth century, so a millennium-scale proxy record gives a much longer baseline against which modern behavior can be judged.

The caveat is that a proxy reconstruction is not a perfect thermometer and one record does not eliminate model uncertainty. What it adds is a stronger historical constraint: the recent ENSO regime looks unusual not merely relative to the satellite era, but relative to many centuries of natural variability.

sections.title: Geopolitics and political economy
sections.content:
• Niger's military regime is now facing an armed challenge from inside the same security apparatus on which its legitimacy rests. Mutinous soldiers attacked Niamey's airport and presidency on Saturday, knocking state television and radio briefly off air and triggering hours of gunfire and explosions. Loyalists had secured the palace by late morning, but the airport remained contested later in the day and the overall situation was still unclear. The deeper problem is institutional: the 2023 coup justified itself partly on the promise of defeating jihadist insurgencies, yet repeated frontline losses are now feeding frustration inside the army itself. If the regime must divert troops and attention toward internal policing, the armed groups it was meant to defeat gain room to operate. Reuters

  • The new Venezuela–US oil framework looks less like ordinary sanctions relief than a 25-year political bargain over capital, operational control and state revenue. Interim President Delcy Rodríguez says the agreement targets more than 1.5 million barrels per day from 17 strategic fields plus eight greenfield blocks, while preserving Venezuelan ownership of the resource. Donald Trump has described the US side in much stronger control terms, saying it secured majority control over more than 65 billion barrels through a public–private arrangement. Those descriptions are not identical, and the detailed contracts are still emerging. The mechanism to watch is therefore the governance structure: who owns the reserves is legally different from who controls investment, production rights, offtake and cash flows over a quarter-century. Reuters

  • Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan are about to test whether their new collective-defence pact becomes an operating institution rather than a declaration. Foreign and defence ministers plus chiefs of staff are due in Istanbul on Monday for the first committee meeting under the 7 August Mecca Joint Defence Agreement, whose mutual-defence clause treats an armed attack on one as an attack on all. The agenda includes interoperability, military capabilities and joint defence-industry production. That is the consequential step: Article-5-style wording has limited value unless it becomes staff planning, procurement rules, communications procedures and actual force compatibility. Reuters

  • A proposed global defence bank is trying to move rearmament from annual budgets onto a multilateral balance sheet. The Defence, Security and Resilience Bank wants roughly €100 billion of lending and guarantees, with Canada and eight other countries currently backing it. Only around €5 billion had been committed by August against a target of €20 billion paid-in capital plus €80 billion callable capital, while Germany and Britain have not joined. The financial engineering is straightforward: sovereign backing could let the bank borrow cheaply and extend lower-cost finance or guarantees to governments and smaller defence suppliers. The unresolved political question is whether enough highly rated states will contribute capital to secure the desired AAA rating, especially when the EU's SAFE programme and Britain's proposed Multilateral Defence Mechanism already compete for the same policy space. Reuters

sections.title: Marxist fragment: Engels on authority, coordination and coercion
sections.content:
“A revolution is certainly the most authoritarian thing there is”

— Friedrich Engels, On Authority (written 1872, published 1874). Primary text

Engels is arguing against socialists who treat authority as a single moral category that can simply be abolished by declaration. His examples range from industrial coordination to revolutionary coercion: collective activity imposes material constraints, and a victorious revolution necessarily imposes one class's will on its opponents.

The useful part of the argument is also where its danger lies. Engels is right that the word authority can hide distinct mechanisms — technical coordination, delegated decision-making and armed coercion are not the same thing, but none disappears because we dislike the label. Yet the essay can slide too quickly from “some synchronized production requires binding decisions” to “political subordination is therefore generally necessary.” A libertarian-socialist reply can accept the first point while insisting that who controls the coordinating authority, how revocable it is, and whether coercion persists after the emergency remain separate political questions. The fragment is strongest as a demand for sharper categories, not as a blank cheque for hierarchy.

sections.title: Two philosophy and political fragments
sections.content:
Locke: law can be infrastructure for freedom rather than its opposite

“the end of law is not to abolish or restrain, but to preserve and enlarge freedom”

— John Locke, Second Treatise of Government, §57. Text

Locke's target is the idea that freedom simply increases whenever rules disappear. His account is relational: without public rules against violence and arbitrary interference, one person's unconstrained power becomes another person's dependence. Law can therefore increase the usable domain of freedom by making other people's coercion less available.

The obvious pressure point is that Locke's conclusion depends on the law itself not becoming arbitrary power. “Rule of law” and “more law” are not synonyms. The argument works only when rules are general enough, public enough and institutionally constrained enough that they reduce domination rather than relocate it into the state.

Kant: permanent military readiness can itself become a cause of war

“Standing Armies shall be entirely abolished in the course of time.”

— Immanuel Kant, Perpetual Peace, Preliminary Article 3. Wikisource

Kant's mechanism is a security dilemma before the modern term existed. A permanently mobilized army makes neighboring states feel threatened; they respond by expanding their own forces; the costs rise without a natural ceiling; and at some point a preventive war can look cheaper than sustaining the competition indefinitely. He also objects to treating paid soldiers as instruments to kill or be killed at another's command.

This is not a proposal for immediate unilateral disarmament. Kant explicitly distinguishes standing armies from periodic voluntary military exercise by citizens for defence. The interesting claim is narrower: a capability built for deterrence can alter everyone else's incentives in ways that manufacture the threat it was built to deter.

sections.title: French usage: carrément
sections.content:
Carrément is a very common familiar intensifier. Larousse gives the colloquial sense “complètement”, alongside the older sense of doing or saying something frankly and categorically. Larousse

  • C'est carrément mieux comme ça. → “It's way / definitely better like this.”
  • Il m'a carrément dit non. → “He flat-out told me no.”
  • Tu veux qu'on y aille maintenant ? — Carrément. → “Want to go now? — Absolutely / totally.”

The standalone answer is especially conversational. Carrément is stronger and more casual than tout à fait; it often adds the speaker's attitude, not just logical agreement. In everyday speech, translating it literally as “squarely” is usually wrong.

sections.title: Music corner
sections.content:
1. Classical: Max Bruch — Romanze in F major for viola and orchestra, Op. 85 — Miles Hoffman
    About 9½ minutes. Bruch is already a strong melodic anchor for you, but this changes both scale and solo colour from the familiar First Violin Concerto: one compact arc built around the viola's darker register, with the same kind of long-breathed late-Romantic melody and harmonic arrival points. It also answers the recent request to keep shorter classical works in rotation without turning the section into “short pieces only.”

  2. Jazz: Dave Grusin — “Mountain Dance” — live at Record Plant, Los Angeles, 1985
    6:10. This sits near the Dan Siegel / Yellowjackets side of your positive results: polished 1980s fusion, but with a clearly stated piano theme and a live arrangement that keeps handing material between Grusin, Lee Ritenour, Dave Valentin and the rhythm section. The bet is that the harmonic clarity and ensemble development will matter more than the period production.

  3. Other: Parcels — “Tieduprightnow” — official video
    4:09. A cleaner pop-facing test of the lane that worked with Cortex and L'Impératrice: bass-forward disco/funk vocabulary, tight guitar-keyboard interlock and a chorus that grows out of the groove rather than interrupting it. It is deliberately more song-structured than the recent psych/funk and electronic picks, so it tests whether the underlying harmonic/groove preference survives a more conventional vocal form.

sections.title: Unrelated fact: some painters literally used Egyptian mummies as pigment
sections.content:
For several centuries, “mummy brown” could be a literal description of an artist's pigment. European colour makers ground material from Egyptian mummies and mixed it into a brown paint used for glazes, shadows and flesh tones. The practice sat downstream of a much older European trade in mumia: substances associated with mummified bodies had already been consumed as medicine, so using human remains as a material input did not initially strike every buyer as a category error. Science History Institute

Demand survived surprisingly late. Art UK documents a 1904 paint firm publicly seeking a 2,000-year-old mummy because supplies were becoming difficult, and Roberson & Co. kept “mummy brown” in its catalogue into the twentieth century; the firm's last tube made from actual mummy material was reportedly produced in 1964. Modern paints sold under similar colour names are mineral formulations instead. The useful correction is that “mummy brown” was never one perfectly standardized recipe and not every brown paint with the name necessarily contained human remains — but the underlying trade was real, commercial and long-lived. Art UK

sections.title: Puzzle: Traveler's Dilemma
sections.content:
Traveler's Dilemma

Two travelers have identical damaged antiques. An airline manager asks each traveler, separately and with no communication, to write an integer from $2 to $100.

  • If both write the same number, both receive that amount.
  • If the numbers differ, the lower number becomes the base payment.
  • The traveler who wrote the lower number gets the base plus $2.
  • The traveler who wrote the higher number gets the base minus $2.

Example: if you write 46 and the other traveler writes 100, you receive 48 and they receive 44.

What number do you write? Then answer a slightly different question: what number do you predict a perfectly reasoning opponent will write? Try to keep those two questions separate before looking up the standard analysis.

Kaushik Basu introduced the game in 1994 specifically to expose tension between intuitive payoff-seeking and standard game-theoretic reasoning. Original paper metadata
